title: Processes and keeping software current
objective: By the end of this lesson you can see what is running on a machine, stop something that should not be, and keep the system patched — which is the highest-value security work most people never do.

blocks.text: A program sitting on disk is a file. A program that is running is a process — it has an id, an owner, memory of its own, and a parent that started it. Knowing what is running, and as whom, is the first question in almost every investigation.

blocks.caption: Seeing what is running
lines: ps aux            # every process: user, PID, CPU, memory, command
ps aux | head     # just the first few lines while you learn the columns
top               # live view, updates continuously (q to quit)
kill 4821         # ask process 4821 to shut down cleanly
kill -9 4821      # force it — last resort, no chance to clean up

blocks.text: The two columns to read first

In ps aux output, the first column is the user the process is running as, and the second is the PID — the process id you would use to stop it. Everything else is detail. The user column is the security-relevant one: a process running as root can do anything root can do.

blocks.title: The question an investigator asks
blocks.text: Not "what is running?" but "what is running as a user that surprises me?". A backup job running as root is expected. A web server process running as root is a finding, because a flaw in that web server now gives an attacker the whole machine rather than one confined account.

Add & to the end of a command to run it in the background, then use jobs to list what you started and fg to bring one back. Useful when you want to start something long-running and keep working in the same terminal.

Linux does not install software by downloading an installer from a website. It uses a package manager that pulls signed packages from repositories the distribution trusts, resolves dependencies, and keeps a record of what is installed.

blocks.caption: On Debian and Ubuntu
lines: sudo apt update              # refresh the list of what is available
sudo apt upgrade             # install available updates
sudo apt install nmap        # install a package
apt list --installed         # what is on this machine
sudo apt remove nmap         # remove it

blocks.text: On Red Hat family systems the same steps are dnf check-update, dnf upgrade, and dnf install. The concepts are identical; only the command name changes.

blocks.title: apt update does not update anything
blocks.text: It refreshes the catalogue of what versions exist. apt upgrade is what actually installs them. Running only the first and believing you have patched the machine is a genuinely common mistake.

blocks.title: Why patching outranks almost everything else
blocks.text: Known vulnerabilities with available fixes remain a common and preventable intrusion path. Package updates remove those known weaknesses; they do not replace defenses against credential abuse, phishing, exposed services or novel vulnerabilities.

blocks.title: Inspect and patch
steps: Run: ps aux | head -15                  (read the USER and PID columns)
Run: ps aux | grep -c ''                (roughly how many processes are running)
Run: sleep 300 &                        (start something in the background)
Run: sudo apt update                    (refresh the catalogue)
Run: apt list --upgradable              (see what is out of date)
blocks.expected: A list of processes with their owners, a background job you start and stop yourself, and a list of packages with updates waiting — often longer than people expect on a machine that has been running a while.

cheatsheet: A process is a running program: it has a PID, an owner, and its own memory
ps aux lists everything · top is the live view · q quits top
Read the USER and PID columns first
A service running as root turns one flaw into total compromise
kill PID asks nicely · kill -9 PID forces (no cleanup)
command & runs in the background · jobs lists · fg brings back
apt update refreshes the catalogue · apt upgrade actually installs
Red Hat family: dnf check-update / dnf upgrade / dnf install
Package updates remove known vulnerabilities for which fixes are available

checkpoint.prompt: In `ps aux` output, which column matters most for a security question?

choices.A: The USER column — who it runs as
choices.B: The terminal it was launched from

checkpoint.explanation: What a process may do is determined by who it runs as. A process running as root can do anything root can do, so an unexpected root process is the thing to explain. What a process may do is determined by who it runs as — an unexpected root process is the thing to explain.

checkpoint.prompt: You ran `sudo apt update` and no packages were installed. Why?

choices.A: The machine is already fully patched anyway
choices.B: apt update only refreshes the catalogue

checkpoint.explanation: Apt upgrade installs them. The two-step model catches people out constantly. update fetches the list, upgrade applies it. Believing the first one patched the machine leaves it unpatched.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is keeping packages current considered high-value security work?

choices.A: Because new versions are always faster
choices.B: Because it replaces the need for permissions
choices.C: It removes known vulnerabilities for which package updates are available
choices.D: Because it satisfies auditors and nothing more

checkpoint.explanation: Package updates close known weaknesses for which maintainers have shipped fixes. That is a concrete risk reduction without making an unsupported claim about what causes most intrusions.
